design_detail: Review article in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry (received 4 March 2007, accepted 24 April 2007; seven printed pages, 87 references) by three authors at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales, Sydney. It calls itself a qualitative review. Aim: to bring together what is known about serotonin syndrome when ecstasy (MDMA) is taken with other serotonergic substances, as a hierarchy of risk for psychiatrists and other doctors. Method (p. 650): a search of Embase, CINAHL, Medline and PubMed and of grey literature to 2006, with the search terms listed in part (a minority taken from ecstasy-related websites); substances were placed in a less, intermediate or high risk group by the proportion of agreement between studies; no comment was made on the quality of any study; national medical and pharmacological experts were consulted when appropriate. No inclusion criteria and no count of records found or used are given. Table 1 (p. 651) sets out the hierarchy. The text cites narrative reviews, case reports, animal studies and surveys.
can_establish: How three authors at a drug research centre grouped serotonergic substances by the risk of serotonin syndrome when taken with ecstasy in 2007; which of the grouped substances have reported human cases (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, phenelzine, from 1987, and a handful of deaths with moclobemide) and which rest on mechanism or animal studies; and what an Australian survey of people who use ecstasy found about deliberate combining with moclobemide and antidepressants, as the review reports it.
cannot_establish: How often any mix causes serotonin syndrome or death (no rates, counts or denominators); that the order of the hierarchy is the order of risk in people, because the groups are the authors’ judgment from an unreported tally with no appraisal; that mixes in the less-risk group are safe (the review says only less likely to produce life-threatening serotonin levels); or anything about the amounts, strengths or timing at which a mix becomes dangerous.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Records from four databases and grey literature to 2006; how many were found or used is not stated. The human evidence cited for the high-risk group is one case series of four deaths (reference 17, Vuori and colleagues, 2003), two older case reports (references 22 and 52) and a survey source (references 54 and 55) by two of the review’s authors; one animal study (reference 53) is cited as further evidence.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated. Search terms ‘included, but were not limited to’ those listed; a minority came from ecstasy-related websites (p. 650).
sample.selection_effects: Cases of serotonin syndrome and death with ecstasy are published because of what happened, and the authors say less serious cases are not usually published, so the extent of non-fatal harm is hard to estimate (p. 652); the groups follow the proportion of agreement between studies with no weighting for design; sources include animal studies, narrative reviews and website posts.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Exposure is as reported in the cited sources, of which only the Vuori case series and three reviews were read for this library; the survey figures (about one in 25 people deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide) are self-reports, cited from a technical report by two of the review’s authors.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. The review gives no doses as findings. It says high doses or repeated use of ecstasy and its analogues intensify serotonin release (reference 40, not read) and gives an 80% loss of brain serotonin within four hours of intravenous use (reference 16, species not stated).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable; the review is about combinations. It says people who use ecstasy tend to use other illicit drugs with serotonergic potency on the same occasions, with alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine frequently combined with ecstasy (p. 652, references 77 and 84 to 87).

comparison.controls: No comparison group. The hierarchy ranks groups of substances against each other by the authors’ reading of the literature; two volunteer studies of ecstasy with citalopram (references 32 and 33, effects of ecstasy reduced) are cited in the less-risk section.

outcomes.instruments: Serotonin syndrome as defined in the cited sources. The review cites the Hunter criteria (reference 24) for the description of signs but states no criteria for deciding which reports in the grouped studies were serotonin syndrome; its discussion refers to case reports that fit the diagnostic criteria for the syndrome (p. 652).
outcomes.operationalization: Four groups in Table 1: less risk, intermediate risk, high risk and unknown risk. The first three are said to follow the proportion of agreement between studies (p. 650); no thresholds or counts are given.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Table 1 (p. 651, checked on a page render): less risk, SSRIs (citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants (clomipramine, imipramine), opioid analgesics (tramadol, dextromethorphan) and antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine), grouped as serotonin reuptake inhibitors; intermediate risk, amphetamine (dexamphetamine, and ‘ethylphenidate’ as printed), amphetamine derivatives (methamphetamine) and cocaine, grouped as serotonin releasers, and 5-HTP and L-tryptophan, grouped as serotonin precursors; high risk, MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, nialamide, isoniazid, clorgyline) and RIMAs (moclobemide), grouped as inhibitors of serotonin metabolism; unknown risk, Saint John’s wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs (dihydroergotamine, bromocriptine) and lithium. Figures in the text: about one in 25 people in a recent Australian study (reference 54) reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide, no denominator given; cases with phenelzine reported from 1987; a handful of documented cases with fatalities for moclobemide (reference 17); susceptibility to an interaction up to 2 weeks after stopping a long-acting MAOI (references 26 and 28).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: The groups depend on the proportion of agreement between studies, which cannot be reconstructed: no table links studies to groups, and the number of records is not given. Some placements rest on mechanism and are worded in theory or is expected (5-HTP, L-tryptophan), and Table 1 does not show which entries rest on cases and which on theory.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative grouping of serotonergic substances by risk of serotonin syndrome when taken with ecstasy, built from reviews, a few case reports, animal studies and surveys. The high-risk group (MAOIs and moclobemide) rests on one case series of four deaths, two older case reports, one animal study and mechanism; the less-risk group on a mechanism argument, animal studies and two volunteer studies in which ecstasy’s effects were reduced by citalopram; the intermediate group mostly on mechanism, with 5-HTP placed there although the review says no human cases have been reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake are less likely to lead to life-threatening elevations in serotonin when taken with ecstasy, that inhibitors of monoamine oxidase are ‘most likely to lead to serious increases’ (p. 649), and that findings highlight the importance of screening for ecstasy and other serotonergic substances when prescribing antidepressants (p. 649). Gaps: (1) the order of the groups is a judgment from an unreported tally; (2) the less-risk statement cites a review that does not address ecstasy with reuptake inhibitors, and the volunteer studies measured ecstasy’s effects, not toxicity; (3) the high-risk group’s human evidence is four deaths in one report and two older case reports; (4) the screening recommendation is not a finding of the review.

timeline.event: Smilkstein and colleagues: a case of an MAOI taken with MDMA (reference 22 of this review, as cited; not read).
Kaskey: a possible interaction between an MAOI and ecstasy (reference 52, as cited; not read).
Vuori and colleagues: four deaths with MDMA and moclobemide in Finland, the review’s source for deaths with moclobemide (reference 17).
Gillman: review of MAOIs and opioids that names MDMA as a serotonin releaser that causes fatalities with MAOIs, including moclobemide (reference 26).
Buckley and colleagues state that serotonin-releasing agents might even attenuate the toxicity of an SSRI, citing one of the same volunteer studies of citalopram with MDMA (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source. Its statements about MAOIs and moclobemide trace to one case series read for this library (Vuori and colleagues, 2003) and to Gillman (2005), also read; its less-risk statements trace to reviews and volunteer studies not read, and the later review by Buckley and colleagues (2014) rests on one of the same volunteer studies, so the two are not independent. No newer systematic review of ecstasy taken with each class of serotonergic medicine was read for this library.

funding.funder: The paper originated from a study funded by the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing (p. 653).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed in the pages read.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales, Sydney (p. 649). Two of them (Copeland and Dillon) are authors of references 54 and 55, the source of the one-in-25 figure and of the self-reported effects. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with stated criteria, a count of records and two-reader appraisal for each combination of ecstasy with a class of serotonergic medicine, with each case report checked against the Hunter criteria; poison-centre and emergency-department data with the number of exposures, so that a rate can be stated; and controlled human data for the pairs where only mechanism or animal studies exist.

domains.note: Databases, years and part of the search terms are given (a minority of terms from ecstasy-related websites), but there are no inclusion criteria, no number of records found or used, and the grouping rule (proportion of agreement between studies) is not shown.
The Method says comment on the quality of each study was not made, so reviews, case reports, animal studies and surveys are used side by side.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of the three authors wrote references 54 and 55, the source of the one-in-25 figure and the self-reported effects (reference 54 is a technical report from their centre); one wrote reference 87. The other references are by other groups.
Hedged wording is common (likely, expected, in theory) and some placements are said to rest on mechanism, but Table 1 does not show which entries rest on reports of people and which on theory.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the grouping
domains.note: Null and limiting evidence is stated (no reported human case of serotonin syndrome with 5-HTP; low fatality incidence against use; non-fatal harm hard to estimate), but disagreements between cited sources are not discussed (methylphenidate; tramadol and venlafaxine).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. The search is partly described, but no group can be traced to a count of studies, no study was appraised, and the strongest statements (the high-risk group) rest on one case series, two older case reports, one animal study and reviews. It may be cited for how three authors grouped serotonergic substances by risk with ecstasy in 2007, and for the cases and surveys it points to. It may not be cited for the order of risk as established, for how often any combination causes harm, or for any combination being safe.

key_findings.finding: The abstract gives the aim as bringing together the risk of serotonin syndrome from taking ecstasy with other serotonergic substances into a hierarchy for doctors, from an extensive online database search. Findings: substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake are less likely to lead to life-threatening elevations in serotonin when taken with ecstasy; high doses or repeated use of stimulants such as methamphetamine and cocaine with ecstasy increase the risk, as does pharmaceutical amphetamine with ecstasy; serotonin precursors also influence the course; and substances that inhibit monoamine oxidase are most likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin with ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: Serotonin syndrome is described as a drug-induced toxic state from excess serotonin in the central nervous system, with autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status (references 23 and 24), most likely to appear with rapid onset, usually within 24 hours of introducing a serotonergic substance (reference 25).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, left-hand column, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state

key_findings.finding: The review says people with serotonin syndrome from illicit drugs such as ecstasy usually reach emergency departments with more advanced symptoms, because some early mild signs are generally seen by many people who use ecstasy as part of normal drug effects (reference 20, Parrott 2002).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, same paragraph (beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state)
key_findings.note: A statement with no data in the review; the source cited was not read.

key_findings.finding: The typical picture is agitation or hypervigilance with tremor and exaggerated reflexes; muscle spasms start in the lower limbs and become generalised as toxicity increases; fever, sweating, dilated pupils, fast heart rate and fast breathing become more evident as the syndrome progresses; fixed rigidity develops in severe cases and can impair breathing and raise carbon dioxide; confusion, rigidity and a body temperature above 38.5 °C are said to indicate life-threatening toxicity (references 24 and 26).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, left-hand column, paragraph beginning Typically, the serotonin-toxic person
key_findings.note: The text extraction drops the greater-than sign before 38.5; the printed page image shows it.

key_findings.finding: Method: a review of peer-reviewed and grey literature up to 2006, searching Embase, CINAHL, Medline and PubMed with search terms that included, but were not limited to, those listed; a minority of terms came from ecstasy-related websites; substances were placed in a less, intermediate or high risk group according to the proportion of agreement between studies; comment on the methodological quality of each study was not made; national medical and pharmacological experts were consulted when appropriate.
key_findings.locator: Method, single paragraph (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Numerous substances are said to have been implicated in serotonin syndrome, including several illicit drugs, antidepressants, opioid analgesics, migraine medication and herbal products (references 23 and 27 to 30); when taken with ecstasy they are said to have a potential for increased toxicity and are arranged in the hierarchy of Table 1.
key_findings.locator: Results, Hierarchy of risk, paragraph beginning Numerous substances have been implicated

key_findings.finding: Table 1 groups, for use with ecstasy: less risk (SSRIs, venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, the opioid analgesics tramadol and dextromethorphan, and antihistamines, all labelled serotonin reuptake inhibitors); intermediate risk (amphetamine and its derivatives and cocaine, labelled serotonin releasers; 5-HTP and L-tryptophan, labelled serotonin precursors); high risk (MAOIs and the RIMA moclobemide, labelled inhibitors of serotonin metabolism); and unknown risk (Saint John’s wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs and lithium).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake (SSRIs, venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, tramadol and dextromethorphan, and antihistamines) are said not to be likely to raise serotonin to life-threatening levels when taken with ecstasy (references 23, 26 and 31), because they compete with MDMA at the serotonin receptor site and so lessen its effects (references 23 and 31).
key_findings.locator: Results, Less risk, 1st paragraph (beginning Substances that inhibit serotonin re-uptake are not likely)
key_findings.note: Reuptake inhibitors act at the serotonin transporter, not a receptor; the wording is loose. See the reporting issues for what the cited sources address.

key_findings.finding: Controlled studies are said to find that the physiological and subjective effects of ecstasy are substantially reduced in participants given citalopram (references 32 and 33); animal experiments are said to show that some SSRIs block MDMA-induced serotonin release (references 31 and 34 to 36), and some animal evidence that some SSRIs may protect against long-lasting neurotoxic effects of MDMA (references 36 to 38); whether this holds in people is said to be yet to be determined.
key_findings.locator: Results, Less risk, 2nd paragraph (beginning Controlled studies have found)

key_findings.finding: Bupropion is said to be devoid of clinically significant serotonergic effects (reference 39), so that taking it with ecstasy is unlikely to increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Results, Less risk, 3rd paragraph (beginning Bupropion, initially used; it ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 651)

key_findings.finding: Intermediate risk: because severity depends on the type and quantity of the substance (reference 23), ecstasy, a potent releaser of serotonin, with other releasers or precursors is said to be likely to carry a greater risk of serious serotonin syndrome; high doses or repeated use of ecstasy and its analogues intensify serotonin release (reference 40); serious serotonergic symptoms are said to have been reported more often when ecstasy is taken with amphetamine and cocaine (reference 41, an emergency-department study by its title; not read).
key_findings.locator: Intermediate risk, 1st paragraph (beginning Because the severity of serotonin syndrome depends), left-hand column

key_findings.finding: Dexamphetamine and methylphenidate (Table 1 prints ethylphenidate) are said to be relatively potent serotonin releasers with some reuptake inhibition (references 29 and 42), as is methamphetamine; amphetamine and MDMA are said to have clinically relevant serotonergic potency, and taking them together is said to be likely to raise the risk (reference 43); cocaine is described as a serotonin releaser that may strongly influence the course of serotonin syndrome, possibly more so with ecstasy (references 25, 28 and 43).
key_findings.locator: Intermediate risk, paragraphs beginning The pharmaceutical stimulants dexamphetamine and The illicit drug cocaine, left-hand column

key_findings.finding: 5-HTP: a review is cited as finding no reported human cases of serotonin syndrome from 5-HTP (reference 49, by its title a review of fibromyalgia and the serotonin pathway; not read), with deaths from overdose in animals (reference 50, dogs by its title); the review says 5-HTP has shown serotonergic potency and that its use with ecstasy is in theory likely to precipitate the syndrome. L-tryptophan is said to have shown serotonergic potency and the risk to be likely to rise if it is combined with ecstasy, especially if taken beforehand (references 23, 28, 30 and 51).
key_findings.locator: Intermediate risk, paragraphs beginning The serotonin precursor 5-hydroxy tryptophan and The serotonin precursor L-tryptophan, right-hand column

key_findings.finding: High risk: taking ecstasy with MAOI antidepressants (phenelzine, tranylcypromine), other MAOIs (nialamide, isoniazid, clorgyline) or the RIMA moclobemide is said to be likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin (references 17 and 26), because these drugs reduce or prevent the enzyme that breaks down serotonin and other neurotransmitters.
key_findings.locator: High risk, 1st paragraph (beginning The use of ecstasy with MAOI antidepressants), right-hand column

key_findings.finding: Cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy with phenelzine are said to have been reported as early as 1987 (references 22 and 52); ecstasy with moclobemide is said to be able to give rise to fatalities, with a handful of cases documented (reference 17, the Vuori case series read for this library: four deaths); further evidence that moclobemide raises the likelihood of severe serotonin syndrome with ecstasy is said to come from animal studies (reference 53).
key_findings.locator: High risk, 2nd paragraph (beginning Cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy interactions with phenelezine; it continues at the top of the left-hand column of p. 652)

key_findings.finding: The long half-life of some MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) is said to mean that a person could still be susceptible to interactions with ecstasy up to 2 weeks after stopping the drug class (references 26 and 28).
key_findings.locator: High risk, same paragraph (continuation at the top of the left-hand column)
key_findings.note: A text search of Gillman (2005, reference 26, read for this library) finds no mention of weeks or half-life; Ener and colleagues (reference 28) were not read. Recorded as the review’s statement, not used for a claim.

key_findings.finding: A recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy (reference 54, a technical report by two of the review’s authors) is cited as finding that about one in 25 reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide, which participants regarded as a way to strengthen ecstasy’s effects or ease the recovery period; the study (reference 55) also found that deliberately taking antidepressants with ecstasy went with a greater likelihood of reporting potentially serious effects such as muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and profuse sweating.
key_findings.locator: High risk, paragraph beginning In a recent Australian study (left-hand column)
key_findings.note: No sample size, recruitment method or time frame is given in the review.

key_findings.finding: Unknown risk: Saint John’s wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs (dihydroergotamine, bromocriptine) and lithium are said to have serotonergic properties or to have been implicated in serotonin syndrome, but whether they carry clinically relevant serotonergic potency, or can cause life-threatening symptoms, is said not to be established; the anti-migraine risk is called more a theoretical concern.
key_findings.locator: Unknown risk, four paragraphs (beginning The herbal extract Saint John’s wort, Lysergic acid, Anti-migraine drugs and Relatively little is known about the mechanism of action of lithium)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the authors say only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-induced harm or death that fit the diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome have been described since the late 1980s (references 17 and 18); that the incidence of ecstasy-related fatalities seems low compared with the likely frequency of use (references 67 to 70) but the extent of acute non-fatal harm is harder to estimate, because less serious cases are not usually published and people in distress use a range of services; and that fatalities from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy overdose alone are relatively rare, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater when ecstasy is taken with other serotonergic drugs or substances.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (begins at the foot of the left-hand column and ends in the right-hand column, before Based on available evidence)

key_findings.finding: The review says evidence is emerging that serotonergic medicines and supplements are deliberately combined with ecstasy to get a specific effect, in some cases with serious consequences (references 17 and 55); anecdotal information from ecstasy-related websites suggests this is not uncommon (references 82 and 83); the medicines named are SSRIs, MAOIs, 5-HTP, Saint John’s wort and pharmaceutical amphetamine (references 55 and 78); and people who use ecstasy tend to use other serotonergic illicit drugs on the same occasions, with alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine frequently combined with ecstasy (references 77 and 84 to 87).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Emerging evidence that a range of serotonergic pharmaceutical drugs (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Implications: the authors say interactions between ecstasy, other illicit drugs and medicines remain largely under-researched, and that the findings highlight the importance of screening for ecstasy and other serotonergic substances when prescribing antidepressants.
key_findings.locator: Implications for intervention, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A recommendation of the authors, not a finding of the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The groups follow the proportion of agreement between studies (p. 650), but no study counts, thresholds or table linking studies to groups are given, the number of records found or used is not stated, and the text cites narrative reviews and animal studies beside case reports. The Method says the quality of each study was not commented on.
reporting_issues.consequence: The order less, intermediate, high is the authors’ judgment, and a reader cannot check it from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The high-risk group cites, for human evidence, one case series of four deaths (reference 17, read for this library), two older case reports (references 22 and 52, by their titles) and a survey source (references 54 and 55), with an animal study (reference 53) and two reviews (references 26 and 28) for mechanism; the phrase a handful of cases stands for the single cited series.
reporting_issues.consequence: The strongest statement in the review rests on a few reports with no count of how many people took the combination, so it cannot give a rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The less-risk statement cites two reviews by one author (references 23 and 26) and a rat study (reference 31). Gillman (2005, reference 26, read for this library) mentions MDMA only as a releaser taken with MAOIs and in Table 1, and does not discuss it with reuptake inhibitors. The two controlled studies cited (references 32 and 33) are said to show reduced effects of ecstasy, not reduced toxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The placement rests on a mechanism argument, animal data and volunteer studies of effects, not on reports of people who took each pair; the statement says less likely, not safe. The wording competing at the serotonin receptor site also does not name the transporter where reuptake inhibitors act.

reporting_issues.issue: Tramadol and venlafaxine are placed in the less-risk group as reuptake inhibitors that lessen ecstasy’s effects, while Gillman (2005, p. 436), cited for the group, calls both anomalous and says they may also act as serotonin releasers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The placement of these two with SSRIs rests on the reuptake argument alone; no data on either with ecstasy are cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls dexamphetamine and methylphenidate relatively potent serotonin releasers (references 29 and 42), while Table 1 prints ethylphenidate as an example of the amphetamine group and Gillman (2005, p. 436, reference 26) calls methylphenidate a weak releaser, citing the same Feinberg review (reference 42 here).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 has a printing error (ethylphenidate is a different drug), and the two papers describe methylphenidate differently, which the review does not mention.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that a person could remain susceptible up to 2 weeks after stopping a long-acting MAOI cites Gillman (2005) and Ener and colleagues (2003); a text search of Gillman (2005) finds no mention of weeks or half-life; Ener and colleagues were not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the 2-week figure could not be traced in the cited paper read for this library, so it is not used for a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-in-25 figure for deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide comes from a technical report by two of the review’s authors (reference 54) and is given with no sample size, recruitment method or time frame; the self-reported effects come from a second paper by the same authors (reference 55).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be read as how common the practice is among people who use ecstasy in general.

reporting_issues.issue: The 80% loss of brain serotonin within four hours of intravenous use is given with no species and with a pharmacology review (reference 16, not read) as the source.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader may take it as a human figure; the review does not say where it comes from.

verification.source_read: PDF (cover page plus printed pp. 649 to 655: abstract, introduction, method, results, Table 1 (checked on a page render), discussion, implications, acknowledgements and reference list). Of the 87 cited sources, four (references 17, 24, 26 and 27: Vuori, Dunkley, Gillman and Boyer) were read for this library; the others were not.
